blocks.text: 1. The Convolution Operation

blocks.alt: A small filter slides across the image, producing a feature map

blocks.text: Image Representation, the previous topic, described how an image becomes a grid of numbers. The Convolution Operation is the foundational computation that respects an image's spatial structure directly, covered in full depth throughout this topic.
It works by sliding a small window across the image, computing a weighted sum at each position, giving this entire architecture family its own distinctive name.
2. The Core Idea

blocks.alt: A small local patch produces a weighted sum, giving a single output value

blocks.text: The genuinely core idea connects back to spatial structure mattering, already covered in Image Representation. Instead of connecting to every pixel at once, look at only a genuinely small, local neighborhood.
This directly addresses the fully-connected-layer problem already covered in that earlier topic, processing an image piece by piece rather than all at once as one giant, flattened vector.
3. The Sliding Window

blocks.alt: A filter slides one step at a time, covering the entire image

blocks.text: This connects back to a small window, already covered in this topic. That small window, called a filter, covered further in the very next topic, slides across the entire image, one position at a time.
It examines every local neighborhood in turn, systematically covering the entire image one small region at a time rather than processing everything simultaneously.

blocks.text: 4. The Weighted Sum Computation

This connects back to weights, already covered throughout Backpropagation & Optimization. At each position, the filter's own values get multiplied by the underlying pixel values, then everything gets summed together.

That single sum becomes one value in the output, called a feature map, covered further later in this module, with the entire feature map built up one such value at a time as the filter slides across the image.
5. Parameter Sharing

blocks.alt: The same filter weights get reused at every position

blocks.text: A genuinely important, distinctive property follows directly. The exact same filter, already covered in this topic, gets reused at every single position, rather than learning a genuinely separate set of weights for each location.

This produces genuinely far fewer parameters than a fully connected layer would need, already covered as impractical in Image Representation, making convolutional layers genuinely efficient even on large images.

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: Parameter sharing, already covered in this topic, is the single biggest reason Convolutional Neural Networks can process large, high-resolution images efficiently, unlike the fully connected approach already covered as impractical in Image Representation.

blocks.text: 6. Translation Invariance

blocks.alt: A feature anywhere in the image still gets detected the same way

blocks.text: This connects back to parameter sharing, already covered in this topic. A pattern learned in one part of the image gets genuinely recognized anywhere else it appears too, since the same filter applies everywhere.

This is called translation invariance, a genuinely valuable property for real image data, where a genuinely meaningful object or pattern, like an edge or a texture, can legitimately appear at any position within an image.
7. A One-Dimensional Convolution Analogy
A genuinely helpful simplification connects back to sequences, a genuinely simpler one-dimensional case covered later in this course through Recurrent Neural Networks and related architectures.

It uses the exact same sliding, weighted-sum idea already covered in this topic, just along a single dimension instead of two, a genuinely useful mental model for understanding the two-dimensional image case already covered throughout the rest of this topic.
8. Why The Output Genuinely Shrinks

blocks.alt: A filter cannot center on edge pixels, producing a smaller output

blocks.text: A genuinely important, real consequence follows. This connects back to the sliding window not fitting past the image's own edges, already covered in this topic. The filter simply cannot center itself right at the very border.
The output feature map is genuinely smaller than the original input, unless padding, covered in the next topic, gets used to compensate for this genuinely real, mechanical edge effect.

blocks.text: 9. Recognizing Why The Convolution Operation Is Genuinely Foundational

blocks.alt: Convolution is the foundation of every CNN

blocks.text: This connects back to every remaining Convolutional Neural Network topic in this module. Every one of them builds directly on this exact sliding, weighted-sum computation already covered here.
Detecting local, genuinely spatial patterns like edges and textures is another genuine case where the Convolution Operation, already covered, is genuinely well suited to exactly this kind of task.
10. Worked Example
The example below directly demonstrates a genuinely simple 2D convolution by hand, sliding a small filter across a small image and computing the weighted sum at each position.

code.content:
import numpy as np

image = np.array([
    [1, 2, 3, 0],
    [4, 5, 6, 1],
    [7, 8, 9, 2],
    [1, 1, 1, 1],
])

filter_kernel = np.array([
    [1, 0],
    [0, -1],
])  # a genuinely simple filter, already covered as the sliding window in this topic

output_size = image.shape[0] - filter_kernel.shape[0] + 1  # already covered as why the output genuinely shrinks
output = np.zeros((output_size, output_size))

for i in range(output_size):
    for j in range(output_size):
        region = image[i:i + 2, j:j + 2]
        output[i, j] = np.sum(region * filter_kernel)  # the weighted sum, already covered in this topic

print("Input image shape:", image.shape)
print("Filter shape:", filter_kernel.shape)
print("Output feature map shape (genuinely smaller than input, already covered in this topic):", output.shape)
print("Output feature map:\n", output)

blocks.title: info
blocks.content: Running this example shows the output feature map is a 3x3 grid from a 4x4 input, exactly the shrinking already covered in this topic, since the 2x2 filter cannot fully center itself at the very last row or column.

blocks.text: 11. Key Takeaways

items: The Convolution Operation slides a small window across an image, computing a weighted sum at each position.
It examines only small, local neighborhoods rather than the entire image at once.
The same filter, or set of weights, gets reused at every single position, called parameter sharing.
This produces far fewer parameters than a fully connected layer would need on the same image.
Translation invariance means a learned pattern gets recognized anywhere it appears in the image.
A one-dimensional convolution applies the same sliding, weighted-sum idea along a single dimension.
The output feature map is smaller than the input unless padding compensates for edge effects.
